## THE CURRENT MAP
68:26/q01 Who owned the garden before these people? [رَأَوْهَا · reports]
  68:26/q01/p1 It belonged to a righteous man, who left it to his people and town. — reasons: Bint al-Shati reports this as part of the exegetes' elaboration of the garden story.
68:26/q02 Where or among whom do reports place the garden? [رَأَوْهَا · reports] (turns on: The reported settings differ; the note gives no grounds for choosing among them.)
  68:26/q02/p1 In Yemen near Sana'a. — reasons: Bint al-Shati lists this among the reported settings, alongside Abyssinia and the People of Scripture.
  68:26/q02/p2 In Abyssinia. — reasons: Bint al-Shati lists this as another reported setting.
  68:26/q02/p3 Among the People of Scripture. — reasons: Bint al-Shati lists this as another reported association.
68:26/q03 How soon did they speak after seeing it? [فَلَمَّا رَأَوْهَا قَالُوٓا۟ · grammar]
  68:26/q03/p1 They spoke immediately and instinctively on seeing it. — reasons: Ibn Ashur says the answer to لما follows its condition immediately.
68:26/q04 What does the plural attribution of their words show? [قَالُوٓا۟ · rhetoric]
  68:26/q04/p1 All the owners agreed about the cause of their misfortune. — reasons: Ibn Ashur draws this from the plural attribution and relates it to the owners in 68:17.
68:26/q05 What did they mean by 'We are astray'? [إِنَّا لَضَآلُّونَ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the destroyed orchard made them think they had taken a wrong road, or they already recognized moral error; the moral readings differ over excluding the poor, straying from truth, and ingratitude.)
  68:26/q05/p1 They thought they had lost the road and arrived somewhere other than their garden. — reasons: Muqatil, Qatada as reported by Abd al-Razzaq, al-Tabari, al-Jishumi, al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi, and Ibn Abbas as reported by Ibn Kathir and al-Durr give the wrong-road sense. Al-Farra and al-Tabari say another brother recognized the garden. Al-Zajjaj, al-Nahhas, al-Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi connect their mistake to its burned, blackened or ruined condition. Al-Mawardi calls it bare; al-Biqa'i says there was no trace of crop or fruit and it no longer resembled their orchard. Al-Baydawi and al-Islahi stress their initial failure to recognize it. Al-Baghawi adds that they had denied the poor and omitted the exception; Ibn Atiyya and al-Zajjaj say they later recognized God's affliction, and al-Razi relates the loss to their miserly resolve. Elmalili says the deprivation exceeded what they had planned for the poor and led to despair of present and future benefit. Ibn Ashur says بل in the next verse corrects their mistaken identification of the site. Al-Tabatabai reports this view but adopts the moral reading; the Study Quran reports it as an alternative and also uses it in its allusion to Muhammad's opponents.
  68:26/q05/p2 They realized that trying to exclude the poor was a moral error and had brought punishment or loss upon them. — reasons: Al-Jishumi reports a reading that they strayed by withholding the poor's due. Al-Razi says they expected to profit from barring the poor but discovered that they themselves were deprived. Al-Qurtubi says they recognized their wrongful dawn plan and the destruction as punishment. Abu Hayyan says their treachery rebounded on them. Al-Tabatabai says they had strayed from right conduct in trying to harvest while excluding the poor and then acknowledged the lost crop. Al-Alusi reports this interpretation but finds it unpersuasive.
  68:26/q05/p3 They recognized that they had strayed from truth or done wrong and were being punished. — reasons: Al-Jishumi reports straying from the truth and being punished for their conduct as an alternative to the specific interpretation about withholding the poor's due. The Study Quran also reports recognition of wrongdoing without specifying its form.
  68:26/q05/p4 They acknowledged straying from gratitude and understood the disaster as punishment for ingratitude. — reasons: Ibn Ashur says the moral use of 'astray' is metaphorical and signals recognition of their failure to thank God.
68:26/q06 Why is their declaration emphatic? [إِنَّا لَضَآلُّونَ · rhetoric]
  68:26/q06/p1 Its emphasis expresses grief and regret at their newly recognized heedlessness. — reasons: Ibn Ashur connects the emphatic form with the freshness of their recognition.
68:26/q07 How did their next words correct this first statement? [لَضَآلُّونَ · links] (turns on: Whether the first words mistook the garden's location or confessed their wrong plan, and thus what the next declaration corrects.)
  68:26/q07/p1 After initially mistaking the ruined garden for another place, they recognized it and said that they had been deprived of its produce and blessing. — reasons: Al-Farra and al-Tabari describe a brother recognizing the garden. Qatada as reported by Abd al-Razzaq and Abu Hayyan, and Ibn Abbas as reported by Ibn Kathir, give the progression from wrong path to deprivation. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi say they recognized punishment; al-Baghawi attributes it to denying the poor and omitting the exception. Ibn Atiyya specifies lost yield and blessing, while al-Razi says their miserly resolve brought the loss. Al-Nasafi says they recognized the garden after looking closely. Elmalili says they found deprivation greater than they intended for the poor, with despair of present and future benefit. Ibn Ashur says بل corrects the location mistake: this was their garden, destroyed and stripped of produce. Al-Islahi says they soon realized their prized possession was gone.
  68:26/q07/p2 After acknowledging their wrong plan, they corrected themselves by saying that they were deprived of the crop. — reasons: Al-Razi says they had expected benefit despite their resolve to bar the poor. Abu Hayyan says 'we are deprived' recognizes that their treachery rebounded on them. Al-Tabatabai says their first words confess straying from right conduct, while the correction names the actual loss.
68:26/q08 What lesson does their reaction to the ruined garden convey? [* · interpretation] (turns on: The notes draw different lessons from the same reaction: repentance through trial, the loss caused by ingratitude, and an analogy to Muhammad's opponents.)
  68:26/q08/p1 A trial can awaken people to their fault and turn them back. — reasons: Ibn Ashur says the owners woke from heedlessness, blamed their pride and failure to thank God, and fulfilled the lesson of 7:168; their quick regret and hope for a better replacement urge repentance.
  68:26/q08/p2 Ingratitude exposes blessings to loss, while gratitude preserves them. — reasons: Ibn Ashur links their lost garden to failure to thank God and quotes Ibn Ata Allah al-Iskandari's maxim that gratitude binds blessings fast.
  68:26/q08/p3 Muhammad's opponents, though thinking themselves guided, will recognize their error and should repent promptly. — reasons: Ibn Ashur says the story urges idolaters to repent as quickly as the owners regretted. The Study Quran relates their initial mistake and eventual recognition to the opponents' mistaken confidence, citing 68:5-7.

## THE NEW NOTES
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهألفازائدةلاينونوكانعلى#564/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | prefers | For four-letter nouns ending in extra non-tanwin alif, the best nisba is -ī, as in ḥublī and daflī, because the alif is not a root letter.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهألفازائدةلاينونوكانعلى#564/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · منهم | reports | Another group adds -āwī to distinguish extra final alif from a root alif, paralleling nouns whose final alif is necessarily extra.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهألفازائدةلاينونوكانعلى#564/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · منهم | reports | A further group says ḥablawī, treating the alif like a root letter because the word is built on it and matches malhā in pattern.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهألفازائدةلاينونوكانعلى#564/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh accepts malhī beside ḥablawī and notes that added and root letters can coincide in nisba when both are fifth.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهألفازائدةلاينونوكانعلى#564/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Forms such as madārī follow the pattern of ḥabālā and ʿadhārā, another way additions and root letters converge.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهألفازائدةلاينونوكانعلى#564/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Qafā does not permit this deletion or extension because it is a three-letter form, not on the pattern of ḥublā.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهألفازائدةلاينونوكانعلى#564/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Jamzā takes jamzī, not jamzawī or jamzāwī, because its weight is heavy and exceeds malhā; the sequential vowels support comparison with ḥubārā.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهألفازائدةلاينونوكانعلى#564/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Deletion is more acceptable in maʿzā than malhā because its alif is extra; ḥublā still best follows the initially stated form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهألفازائدةلاينونوكانعلى#564/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الشاعر | reports | The poetic line uses Baṣrā, not al-Baṣrī, as Sībawayh explicitly explains its intended form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهياءوكانالحرفالذيقبلالياء#561/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In nisba formation, final yāʾ or wāw preceded by a consonant remains unchanged because it behaves like a sound consonant.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهياءوكانالحرفالذيقبلالياء#561/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The unchanged wāw after a silent consonant is supported by the nisba Jirwī from Banū Jurwa.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهياءوكانالحرفالذيقبلالياء#561/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yūnus treats yāʾ-root and wāw-root forms alike in this class and also gives ʿarwī.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهياءوكانالحرفالذيقبلالياء#561/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · من الناس | r

eports | One view forms nisbas from feminine nouns in -iyya with yāʾ, treating the base as a non-defective noun after removing tāʾ marbūṭa.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهياءوكانالحرفالذيقبلالياء#561/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | This yāʾ formation is supported by the behavior of rami and naḥi, which pattern like sound nouns; if Umayya permits it, it is still more apt for ramiya.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهياءوكانالحرفالذيقبلالياء#561/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أبو عمرو | reports | Yūnus reports that Abū ʿAmr used the yāʾ form ẓabiyy for ẓabiyya, which Sībawayh says is the sole analogical form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهياءوكانالحرفالذيقبلالياء#561/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yūnus gives an alternative with wāw for ẓabiyya, damiyya, and fatiyya.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهياءوكانالحرفالذيقبلالياء#561/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl explains the wāw forms as analogies to faʿla: the suffixed forms look like that pattern, whose nisba preserves wāw.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهياءوكانالحرفالذيقبلالياء#561/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | prefers | Al-Khalīl prefers the first, yāʾ-based analysis as more analogical and more idiomatic; he cites Zinwi and Baṭṭawi as parallels.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهياءوكانالحرفالذيقبلالياء#561/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | holds | Al-Khalīl excludes ghazwa and ghadwa from the faʿla analogy because their endings do not match it; their nisbas remain ghazwī and ghadwī.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإضافةإلىكلاسمكانآخرهياءوكانالحرفالذيقبلالياء#561/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | holds | For ʿurwa the form is ʿarwī; when deletion of tāʾ leaves wāw after a silent consonant, the wāw does not change.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيففيبناتالياءوذلكنحوعييتوحييتوأحييت)#795/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Doubled verbs with final yāʾ follow other defective-yāʾ verbs, not ordinary doubled verbs: the yāʾ behaves like the final of yakhshā or yarmī.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيففيبناتالياءوذلكنحوعييتوحييتوأحييت)#795/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Related forms such as maʿiyya, muḥyiyān, maʿiyān, and ḥayyān can be concealed or distinguished; distinction is clearer after kasra because three yāʾs meet.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيففيبناتالياءوذلكنحوعييتوحييتوأحييت)#795/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The form taḥiyya follows the pattern tafʿila, like aḥyiyya.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيففيبناتالياءوذلكنحوعييتوحييتوأحييت)#795/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Doubled yāʾ is rare because final yāʾ is already heavy and a preceding yāʾ makes it heavier.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيففيبناتالياءوذلكنحوعييتوحييتوأحييت)#795/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The form aḥyā is compared with aḥmad and similar sound-root forms because the preceding fatḥa remains fixed, so doubling behaves like madd and wadda. | mentions 8:42
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيففيبناتالياءوذلكنحوعييتوحييتوأحييت)#795/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When the yāʾ is in a position where its movement is obligatory, assimilation is permitted because the final behaves like a sound consonant; assimilation is more common, though the separated form is also Arabic.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيففيبناتالياءوذلكنحوعييتوحييتوأحييت)#795/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الشاعر | reports | A poem with ḥayū witnesses deletion of final yāʾ in the plural, parallel to khashaw and akhshaw.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيففيبناتالياءوذلكنحوعييتوحييتوأحييت)#795/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بعضهم | reports | Some speakers say ḥayū and ʿayū, analogizing the plural to doubled forms found in the singular, dual, and feminine.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيففيبناتالياءوذلكنحوعييتوحييتوأحييت)#795/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الشاعر | reports | The poem ʿayū bi-amrihim, as the dove failed with its egg, witnesses the alternative plural form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيففيبناتالياءوذلكنحوعييتوحييتوأحييت)#795/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yūnus reports many Arabs who keep the two yāʾs distinct in ḥayiya al-rajul and ḥayit al-marʾa rather than treating them as ordinary doubled forms.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيففيبناتالياءوذلكنحوعييتوحييتوأحييت)#795/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بعض العرب | reports | Some Arabs pronounce forms such as aʿyāʾ and aḥyiyya distinctly; Sībawayh says concealment is better, though full distinction is also possible.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيففيبناتالياءوذلكنحوعييتوحييتوأحييت)#795/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In subjunctive forms such as raʾaytu maʿiyyan and yurīdu an yuḥyiyahu, the yāʾs are not assimilated because the movement is not obligatory; concealment is best, but distinction is allowed.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالتضعيففيبناتالياءوذلكنحوعييتوحييتوأحييت)#795/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The Qurʾanic wording a-laysa dhālika bi-qādirin ʿalā an yuḥyiya al-mawtā is evidence against assimilation in this environment. | mentions 75:40
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكسرفيهالهاءالتيهيعلامةالإضمار)#742/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The default pronoun hāʾ is ḍamma followed by wāw; this remains the form unless a stated conditioning environment intervenes.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكسرفيهالهاءالتيهيعلامةالإضمار)#742/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الحطيئة | reports | Al-Ḥuṭayʾa's verse witnesses the Bakr dialect form that assimilates the pronoun hāʾ to a preceding kasra.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكسرفيهالهاءالتيهيعلامةالإضمار)#742/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · هارون | reports | Hārūn identifies the ṣād-to-zāy intermediate pronunciation in ḥattā yaṣdura al-riʿāʾ as al-Aʿraj's and Mecca's current reading. | mentions 28:23
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكسرفيهالهاءالتيهيعلامةالإضمار)#742/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When hāʾ is preceded by a moving consonant, as in qāḍiyahu, it is not kasra because it is no longer a weak letter like unmovable alif.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكسرفيهالهاءالتيهيعلامةالإضمار)#742/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Despite movement, hāʾ remains faint and can count like a still yāʾ or wāw in rhyme, as in khalīluhā and khalīlū.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكسرفيهالهاءالتيهيعلامةالإضمار)#742/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The hāʾ of the feminine demonstrative hādhihi behaves like pronoun hāʾ because both are markers outside the preceding word.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكسرفيهالهاءالتيهيعلامةالإضمار)#742/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | At pause the demonstrative hāʾ is deleted, as in bih and ʿalayh; some Arabs also make it silent in connected speech by analogy with plural mīm.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكسرفيهالهاءالتيهيعلامةالإضمار)#742/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The connected-speech variant is attributed to the fixed kasra and frequency of this form; Sībawayh heard hādhihi ummat Allāh with a silent hāʾ from a trusted speaker.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكسرفيهالهاءالتيهيعلامةالإضمار)#742/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After yāʾ or kasra, hāʾ is kasra and its wāw becomes yāʾ: its lightness resembles yāʾ, and kasra triggers the change as in imāla.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكسرفيهالهاءالتيهيعلامةالإضمار)#742/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أهل الحجاز | reports | The Hijazis retain ḍamma and wāw in forms such as bihu and dāruhu, and are reported to read the cited phrase that way. | mentions 28:81
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكسرفيهالهاءالتيهيعلامةالإضمار)#742/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When hāʾ follows plural mīm, the mīm is kasra to avoid ḍamma after kasra, and the hāʾ's following wāw becomes yāʾ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكسرفيهالهاءالتيهيعلامةالإضمار)#742/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أهل الحجاز | reports | The Hijazis use forms such as ʿalayhumu and bihimu with ḍamma and wāw after plural mīm. | mentions 28:81
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكسرفيهالهاءالتيهيعلامةالإضمار)#742/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بعضهم | reports | Some speakers instead make mīm kasra before the similar yāʾ, while leaving mīm unchanged where it resembles neither yāʾ nor alif.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكسرفيهالهاءالتيهيعلامةالإضمار)#742/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · قوما من ربيعة | reports | Some of Rabīʿa say minhum with hāʾ following kasra even across a still consonant.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكسرفيهالهاءالتيهيعلامةالإضمار)#742/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | rejects | Sībawayh calls the Rabīʿa form poor when a consonant separates hāʾ from kasra; when the vowels are distant, the original form is preferable.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتكسرفيهالهاءالتيهيعلامةالإضمار)#742/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · ناس من بكر بن وائل | rejects | Some Bakr b. Wāʾil speakers assimilate hāʾ after kasra because it is a pronoun marker; Sībawayh judges this dialect very poor.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنياءالإضافةلاتثبتمعالنداءكمالميثبتالتنوينفيالمفرد#300/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In vocatives, the first-person possessive yāʾ is dropped like tanwīn, since it substitutes for tanwīn in the noun.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنياءالإضافةلاتثبتمعالنداءكمالميثبتالتنوينفيالمفرد#300/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl adduces the pause forms yā ummah and yā abah, parallel to yā khālah, as evidence for that analysis.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنياءالإضافةلاتثبتمعالنداءكمالميثبتالتنوينفيالمفرد#300/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The hāʾ is attached especially in vocatives annexed to oneself as compensation for the deleted yāʾ; this is rare outside the vocative.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنياءالإضافةلاتثبتمعالنداءكمالميثبتالتنوينفيالمفرد#300/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Vocative hāʾ marks and reinforces attention like yā; this construction is therefore restricted to the vocative.
